Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale

Hao Kang    Weili Xu    Ziyang Li*    Zheng Du    Hanchen Li    Tian Xia    Song Bian    Tushar Krishna    Huizi Mao    Ion Stoica    Song Han
Abstract

Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill–decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key–value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1×\times and 14×\times over Dynamo, NVIDIA’s production framework.

 

1Georgia Institute of Technology, 2University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
3University of California, Berkeley, 4NVIDIA, 5OpenAI, 6Massachusetts Institute of Technology

1 Introduction

Agentic workloads account for a large and growing share of LLM inference [9, 30], spanning software engineering [22], math research [38], and computer use [5]. Agents execute these tasks in steps, each consisting of a model request and the tool calls it triggers, with harnesses updating the context between steps. Successive requests therefore typically share long prefixes, creating opportunities for key–value (KV) cache reuse across consecutive steps.

These workloads place diverse demands on prefill and decode resources. Differences in tasks, harnesses, and models lead to different amounts of uncached input and generated output per request, making some agent workloads prefill-heavy and others decode-heavy (2(a)). The agent workload composition, i.e., the proportions of different agent workloads served by a cluster, also varies over time. A production study of 11.7 million requests finds that user-triggered task starts follow workday rhythms, whereas automatically triggered task starts are more evenly distributed throughout the day [79]. In prefill–decode (PD) disaggregation, the allocation of nodes (the PD split) that best balances prefill and decode can change as this composition shifts(2(b)).

Meanwhile, within an agent, context management changes which prefixes subsequent requests can reuse. Harnesses compact histories, fork and create sub-agents [7, 47]. Each fork or sub-agent starts a new branch, a context that has its own sequence of requests and remains active until it finishes. A branch waiting for a tool or sub-agent may reuse its existing prefix after a long pause, whereas compaction can remove recently accessed history from the subsequent requests of a branch (2(c)). Access recency alone thus does not reveal which cached prefixes remain useful to active branches.

Serving agents efficiently thus requires adapting compute allocation to diverse agent workloads and their shifting composition, and KV cache management to agent context management. Production systems [40] serve agentic workloads with PD disaggregation [80] and manage compute and memory with three components. A planner determines the compute allocation between prefill and decode by assigning nodes to each phase [42, 69]. A cache-aware router routes each request to a node with matching prefix KV [58, 45]. A memory pool shares and evicts KV across nodes [50, 72]. However, agentic workloads expose three problems in existing systems.

Costly phase switches. Each adaptation of the compute allocation switches nodes between phases, and such switches are expensive in existing systems. Some [42] relaunch serving workers to change their phase, which takes minutes and removes the node from service during the switch. Others switch without a restart [69] but strand the node’s cached KV, forcing later requests to recompute their prefixes. In our measurements on Claude Code traces, Dynamo takes 681 s per switch on average, while Arrow loses 55.5% of the available KV reuse over 34 in-place switches (3(a)).

Misestimated compute demand. A PD split profiled offline for each agent workload is costly to obtain and cannot follow the shifting workload composition. Even the best static split loses up to 24% of throughput in some periods relative to the best split of each 10-minute window (2(b)). Online planners also misestimate demand. They adjust the PD split using coarse signals such as queue depth [42] or predicted time to first token (TTFT) [31]. Context management, such as spawning several sub-agents at once, can create short bursts of prefill work that perturb these signals and trigger costly phase switches without sustained throughput gains. Some planners also estimate prefill work from the full input length [69], ignoring KV reuse and overestimating the number of prefill nodes needed (3(b)).

Misjudged KV reuse. Existing systems misjudge KV reuse when they route requests and evict KV. Requests of the same branch share long prefixes. Cache-aware routers [58] concentrate these requests on the few prefill nodes holding their prefixes, overloading them and raising P95 TTFT. Routers [45] that trade cache locality for load balance can route requests to nodes that must recompute their prefixes. The memory pool avoids this recomputation, but its KV fetches can delay prefill and leave duplicate copies in the pool (3(c)). The memory pool and node caches typically evict KV in least recently used (LRU) order [78, 50]. They thus drop the KV of branches waiting for tools, sub-agents, or users while keeping the history replaced by compaction, the contexts of finished sub-agents, and duplicate copies left by KV transfers.

Two limitations underlie these problems. First, compute allocation and KV cache management remain coupled. Engines index cached KV in local state. Switching a node from prefill to decode thus discards or strands its cached KV. Shared KV pools avoid this coupling, but keep the allocation fixed or change it by relaunching nodes. Second, the three components rely on coarse signals, such as request latency, input lengths, and access history, which do not fully reveal the agent workload or context management. To our knowledge, Evolving Infra is the first agent-adaptive serving framework, adapting compute allocation to diverse agent workloads and their shifting composition, and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We make three contributions.

Decoupled compute allocation and KV cache management. To reduce the cost of phase switches, Evolving Infra separates the phase of each node from the KV storage. Each node supports both phases, and the planner reassigns its phase at runtime without a restart. KV resides in a shared pool formed by the host memory of all nodes, and a cluster-wide KV directory records the number of active branches that reference each copy. Neither the pool nor the directory is tied to node phases, and a phase switch leaves the KV readable by all nodes. The directory updates these counts in response to agent context management and KV transfers between nodes (Section 4).

Agent-adaptive compute allocation. To precisely size the PD split for the agent workload composition, Evolving Infra learns iteration-time models of prefill and decode online, without offline profiling (Section 5.1). The prefill model incorporates KV reuse, enabling accurate estimation of prefill time on agentic workloads. The planner evaluates these models on the average work of a request over each planning window. These averages characterize the workload itself rather than the momentary load of the cluster. The planner switches only when the predicted throughput gain of a new split persists across the window, which keeps short bursts from triggering switches (Section 5.2).

Agent-adaptive KV cache management. To keep the reusable KV of active branches while balancing the load of prefill nodes, Evolving Infra routes requests and evicts KV according to agent context management. It fetches remote KV asynchronously while a request is queued, which allows the router to send each prefill request to the node with the shortest predicted TTFT. The directory shows that no active branch references replaced histories, the contexts of finished sub-agents, or duplicate copies left by transfers, and Evolving Infra evicts this KV first (Sections 4.2, 4.3, and 5.3).

We evaluate Evolving Infra on coding, computer-use and math agents, serving GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on 36 GB300 GPUs. When serving a single agent workload at a stationary load, Evolving Infra achieves up to 2.7×\times the throughput of Dynamo and up to 38% more than the best static split. Reduces the mean end-to-end (E2E) request latency by up to 4.1×\times and P95 TTFT by up to 14×\times relative to Dynamo (Figure 1). For a shifting workload composition from math to computer-use agents, Evolving Infra adapts the PD split online, achieving 2.1×\times the throughput of Dynamo and 28% more than the best static split (Section 6.3).

2 Background

2.1 Diverse and dynamic agentic workloads

Workload composition.

An agent solves a task in steps orchestrated by a harness. Each LLM request appends new tokens from tools or the harness to a prefix whose KV was computed in earlier steps. The inference engine fetches the cached prefix KV, prefills the uncached tokens, and decodes the output tokens. The amounts of prefill and decode work differ across tasks, harnesses, and models. For example, the workload of a computer-use agent on OSWorld is prefill-heavy because each step appends a new screenshot to the context, whereas the workload of a math agent on Putnam is decode-heavy because each request generates a long reasoning trace (2(a)). The best PD split thus differs across agent workloads, and finding it requires costly offline profiling (Section 6.4). The workload composition of a cluster also changes over time. User-triggered agent tasks starts follow workday rhythms, whereas automatically triggered tasks starts are more evenly distributed throughout the day [79]. In production LLM serving, the mean input length of requests to one model rises by 13% from midnight to afternoon, while the mean output length falls by 18% [70]. The best PD split thus shifts over time (2(b)). The PD split must therefore change over time to avoid load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes.

Context management.

The harness typically extends the context of a branch with model outputs and tool results, and consecutive requests therefore share prefixes. Harnesses also manage context through forking, sub-agent spawning, and compaction. Forking creates new branches that reuse the current context, while spawning a sub-agent starts a separate branch with a new context. Compaction replaces the history of a branch with a summary [47, 6]. Once compaction completes, even recently accessed KV of the replaced history is no longer needed. In contrast, KV can remain idle during a long wait for tools or sub-agents, yet still be reused when the branch resumes. In GitHub Copilot, the median gap between consecutive turns is 172 s [30]. Whether KV will be reused thus depends on whether an active branch still includes it in its context, not merely on access recency. Together with the shift in workload composition, these dynamics challenge the planner, the router, and the memory pool of existing serving systems, which the rest of this section reviews.

2.2 Existing PD disaggregated serving systems

Engines.

By default, vLLM and SGLang fix the phase of each engine at launch in PD disaggregation mode [64, 54]. For example, each SGLang engine builds only the scheduling loop and KV transfer path of its own phase. A prefill engine queues requests and sends their KV to decode engines, whereas a decode engine reserves KV slots, receives KV, and captures CUDA graphs for decoding. Each engine also indexes cached KV in local state, such as the prefix tree of a prefill engine. A phase switch thus requires relaunching the engine with a new configuration and discards its cached KV.

Planners.

A planner sets the PD split by switching nodes between prefill and decode as compute demand changes. Phase switches in existing planners are costly. A switch in Dynamo relaunches the engine and keeps the node out of service for minutes [42]. A switch in Arrow [69] and xLLM [31] reassigns the node to the other phase without a relaunch but strands its cached KV. The split also follows coarse signals, namely prefill queue depth and decode KV utilization in Dynamo [42], and TTFT and per-token latency targets in Arrow, xLLM, and Llumnix [32]. These planners predict TTFT from the full input length [69, 31, 33], which counts cached prefixes as prefill work and overestimates prefill demand. Sub-agents spawned at once by the harness create a short burst of requests. The burst raises queueing delay and TTFT but leaves the long-term balance between prefill and decode workloads unchanged. These signals thus misestimate demand and trigger frequent phase switches, each costing minutes of downtime or the cached KV of the switched node (Section 3).

Routers.

A router assigns each request to a prefill and decode node. For prefill, the SGLang Model Gateway and the Dynamo router weigh prefix-cache hits against node load [58, 45]. The Dynamo router keeps a cluster-wide prefix tree that records which KV blocks each node holds, and the engines update the tree through KV events [45]. For each request, the router uses this tree to count the prefix blocks that each node already holds. These routers choose where a request runs but do not move its KV. Without a memory pool, a request thus either queues at a node that holds its prefix, raising TTFT, or recomputes the prefix on another node, lowering throughput.

Memory pools.

A memory pool extends the capacity for reusable KV beyond GPU memory. HiCache caches KV in GPU memory (L1) and host memory (L2) on each node and shares KV across nodes through an optional storage tier (L3), such as Mooncake Store [72, 50]. Shared KV moves from the L2 of the source node through L3 to the L2 of the destination node, leaving copies in L3 and in the L2 of both nodes. HiCache loads the fetched KV into GPU memory only when the request starts its prefill [52]. This load therefore delays prefill and raises TTFT (Section 3.3). These pools index KV by content and typically evict KV in LRU order. LRU eviction thus cannot distinguish the KV of a branch that waits for a tool from the history that compaction has replaced. Agent-aware systems such as Continuum and ThunderAgent retain the KV of agents that wait for tools [27, 23], but assume that each context only grows and do not track the duplicate copies that KV transfers leave across nodes.

In summary, these systems couple compute allocation with KV cache management, making phase switches costly. Their planners rely on coarse signals that do not fully reveal the workload composition, and their routers trade cache locality against load balance. Their memory pools load fetched KV only when prefill starts, evict KV by access recency, and leave duplicate copies after KV transfers. Agent-aware systems retain the KV of waiting agents but assume that contexts only grow. Section 3 quantifies the resulting losses.

3 Motivation

This section profiles PD-disaggregated serving systems on agentic workloads and quantifies three sources of inefficiency, namely costly phase switches, misestimated compute demand, and misjudged KV reuse. We use the testbed of Section 6.1, nine nodes of 4×\timesGB300 GPUs that serve GLM-5.2 with TP4, and replay the Claude Code traces with 90 concurrent agents for one hour after a 30-minute warmup. Dynamo runs its planner at the default throughput target with the SGLang Model Gateway. Arrow’s code is not public, so we reimplement its planner and scheduler on the symmetric engines of Evolving Infra (Section 4.1). Both planners start from 6P3D, and each node runs HiCache with LRU eviction. For routing (Section 3.3), we run SGLang in its PD disaggregation mode at the best static split, 4P5D, and compare the cache-aware and sticky-session policies of the SGLang Model Gateway, the Dynamo KV router [45], and a variant of the Dynamo KV router whose nodes fetch prefixes from a shared host-memory pool (+ memory pool).

3.1 Costly phase switches

Every phase switch takes time, loses KV reuse, or both (3(a)), because engines fix their phase at launch and index cached KV locally (Section 2.2). The Dynamo planner relaunches the worker of a node at every switch. A switch takes 681 s on average, during which the node serves no requests. Arrow switches nodes in place without this delay, but the KV of a switched node becomes unreachable for prefill. Arrow misses 55.5% of the cache hits that it would achieve with an unlimited KV cache shared by all nodes and no phase switches, and Dynamo misses 5.1%. We call this fraction of missed hits the lost KV reuse. Avoiding both costs requires an engine that serves both phases without a relaunch and a KV pool that every node can read in either phase.

3.2 Misestimated compute demand

Both online planners size the split from coarse signals (Section 2). The Dynamo planner and Arrow thus deliver 49% and 65% less throughput than the best static split(4.9 req/s), respectively (3(b)). These signals misjudge the work of agents in opposite directions. Arrow predicts prefill time from the full input length, which counts cached prefixes as work, and it also reacts to short prefill bursts, such as several sub-agents that start together. Arrow thus drifts from 6P3D to 8P1D, and switches 34 times during the run, each time incurring the costs in Section 3.1. The Dynamo planner instead follows queue depth and KV utilization. Long agent contexts keep the KV utilization of decode nodes high, and the planner drifts past 4P5D to 2P7D. Sizing the split well requires a model of the average prefill and decode work that a request needs after KV reuse. Short bursts of sub-agents and forks raise the momentary load but barely change the average.

3.3 Misjudged KV reuse

Routers misjudge the KV reuse of agents in either direction (3(c)). The cache-aware and sticky policies of the SGLang Model Gateway keep an agent and its forked branches on the few prefill nodes that hold their prefixes. The P95 TTFT thus reaches 27 s and 34 s. The load-aware Dynamo KV router [45] sends more requests to nodes that lack their prefixes, which recompute them, and the P95 TTFT reaches 65 s. With the shared memory pool, these nodes fetch the prefixes instead, yet the P95 TTFT rises to 95 s. Because the pool loads the fetched KV into GPU memory only when the request begins its prefill, the load adds to the prefill time instead of overlapping with queueing (Appendix D.6). The duplicate copies that fetches leave also occupy host memory and displace the KV that agents still need.

Eviction misjudges KV reuse as well. HiCache evicts the least recently used KV, whereas the reuse of agent KV depends on whether an active branch still includes it (Section 2). HiCache thus keeps histories that compaction replaced but evicts the KV of branches that wait for tools, sub-agents, or users. On the CC traces, these evictions cause 39% of the KV reuse that Dynamo loses (Appendix C.1). Reusing KV well requires a memory pool that hides fetch delays, routing that balances load, and eviction that follows agent context management and removes duplicate copies.

4 Decoupled and Agent-Aware Infrastructure

This section presents the infrastructure that enables efficient online adaptation (Figure 1). The symmetric engine (Section 4.1) allows nodes to switch phases without a relaunch, and the shared KV pool (Section 4.2) keeps KV readable by all nodes in either phase. Together, they meet the two needs in Section 3.1 and decouple compute allocation and KV cache management. The KV directory (Section 4.3) counts the active branches that reference each KV block on each node and updates these counts as branches fork, compact, or finish and as KV moves between nodes. These counts identify the KV that no active branch reuses (Section 3.3).

4.1 Symmetric engines for online phase switches

To reduce the cost of online prefill–decode phase switches (Section 3.1), we build a symmetric engine that supports both phases, so that every node can serve either phase. With this engine, the router separates prefill and decode at runtime rather than through a static deployment configuration. Unlike SGLang (Section 2), whose prefill and decode engines run different scheduling loops and fix their phase at launch by default, our engine extends SGLang with one scheduling loop that serves both phases and a KV transfer protocol that moves KV between any two nodes in either direction. The protocol reuses the RDMA transport of Mooncake [50] and keeps working after a node switches its phase. Every node of Evolving Infra runs this engine, and a single router routes prefill requests to one set of nodes and decode requests to the remaining nodes (Figure 1). When the planner reassigns the phase of a node (Section 5.2), the router changes the type of requests that it routes to the node, and the engine serves the new phase without a restart.

4.2 Shared host-memory KV pool

To keep KV readable by every node in either phase (Section 3.1), Evolving Infra pools the host memory (L2) of all nodes into a shared KV pool. Following HiCache [72], each node caches KV in GPU memory (L1) and writes it through to its L2 in both phases. A prefill node locates reusable KV through the directory (Section 4.3) and pulls it from the L2 of a peer over RDMA. Unlike the storage tier of SGLang, which stages shared KV in a separate store, the pool reads directly from the L2 of a peer and avoids this extra copy (Appendix A.2). Deduplication across the GPUs of a node further increases its effective capacity (Appendix A.5). Decode nodes only write to the pool, since a fetch from host memory would delay decoding (Appendix D.6). They receive the KV of each request from the prefill node through the faster GPU-to-GPU transfer, and the KV that they generate stays in their L2 for the next request of the branch.

A fetch from a peer, however, delays the prefill of its request (Section 3.3). HiCache prefetches KV only into host memory while a request waits and loads it into GPU memory layer by layer during prefill. Evolving Infra instead completes the whole fetch while the request waits in the queue. The node pulls the KV from the L2 of the peer into its own L2, loads it into GPU memory, and broadcasts it to all GPUs of the node before the prefill begins.

When the planner selects a new split (Section 5.2), the router moves the queued requests of each switching node to other nodes of its current phase. The running requests of the node finish in place, after which the node switches its phase. The KV of the switching node stays in the pool and remains readable by all nodes throughout the switch (Section 3.1).

4.3 Agent-aware cluster-wide KV directory

To identify the duplicate copies that KV transfers leave and the histories that context management drops (Section 3.3), the router (Figure 1) maintains a cluster-wide KV directory. Following the Dynamo KV indexer [45], the directory is a prefix tree that records KV placement in GPU and host memory of each node. The router updates this tree with the KV events that the engines publish (Section 2). The directory also records, for each block on each node, how many active branches reference it (Figure 4).

The router updates these counts from two identifiers. The harness tags each request with the ID of the agent branch that issues it and reports when a branch finishes. The router maintains a version for each branch and increments it when the context of the branch is rewritten. The engine on each node then updates the eviction priority of the KV blocks in its host memory according to the counts that the router sends (Section 5.3).

Both identifiers follow agent context management. When the harness forks a context or spawns a sub-agent, it sends the ID of the new branch to the router. The router then adds one count to each block that the new branch reuses on the node that serves it. For consecutive requests of the same branch, the router compares the new request with the previous request of the branch. If the new request only appends tokens, the router adds counts only to the newly appended blocks on the routed node (4(a)). The reused blocks keep their counts, since the branch was already counted on them in earlier steps. If the context is rewritten by compaction, the router increments the version. It then releases the counts on the blocks that the new context drops and adds counts to the blocks that it newly includes (4(b)). When the harness reports that a branch has finished, the router releases all counts of the branch.

Counts also follow KV transfers. A transfer between two nodes of the same phase (P2P or D2D) moves the counts of the branch, since the branch reuses only the target copy in that phase. The source releases them once the target holds the current version (4(c)). A transfer across phases (P2D or D2P) keeps the counts on both nodes, since the next step of the branch needs the copies in both phases (4(d)). A node that switches from decode to prefill resets its counts to free its memory, whereas a node that switches to decode keeps them to preserve its KV. Appendix E.1 and Appendix E.2 give these rules in pseudocode. As a result, each active branch holds counts on at most one copy per phase.

5 Agent-Adaptive Compute Allocation and KV Cache Management

Based on the infrastructure in Section 4, this section presents how Evolving Infra adapts compute allocation and KV cache management to agents at runtime. We first characterize the work of each request and learn iteration-time models of each node online (Section 5.1). Section 5.2 then presents the planner, which uses these models to size the PD split for diverse agent workloads and their shifting composition. Given the split, Section 5.3 presents KV-reuse-aware eviction and routing, which preserve the KV that active branches still reuse and balance prefill work across nodes. Table 1 summarizes the notation.

5.1 Prefill and decode iteration-time models

As Section 3.2 shows, sizing the split requires a model of the average prefill and decode work that a request needs after KV reuse. This section models how long a request with given work occupies a node, and Section 5.2 evaluates this model on the average work over each planning window. A node runs its requests in iterations, each of which is a forward pass of the model. Under continuous batching [76], each iteration serves a batch of requests, and requests join or leave the batch between iterations. Accurate predictions of iteration time thus allow Evolving Infra to estimate the prefill and decode throughput of each node and the waiting time of prefill requests. For each phase, we model the iteration time from the requests in its batch and derive the number of requests that each node completes per second. We describe each request in a batch by its work w=(tuc,tc,tout,tacc)w=(t_{\mathrm{uc}},t_{\mathrm{c}},t_{\mathrm{out}},t_{\mathrm{acc}}), where Table 1 defines each component. The router obtains tct_{\mathrm{c}} from the longest cached prefix that the KV directory finds for the request (Section 4.3), and tuct_{\mathrm{uc}} counts the remaining input tokens. Separating the two token lengths allows the models to predict prefill time accurately, even when agents reuse most of their context.

The models rest on two premises. First, the kernels of a forward pass run one after another, and the iteration time is the sum of their execution times. Second, as in the roofline model [68], each kernel is limited either by the compute throughput or by the memory bandwidth of the GPU. A compute-bound kernel runs in time proportional to its arithmetic operations, whereas a memory-bound kernel runs in time proportional to the bytes that it reads and writes.

Prefill iteration-time model. Prefill spends most of its time in compute-bound kernels [80]. Under chunked prefill [1], each prefill iteration processes the uncached tokens of several requests up to a fixed token budget. The execution time of the linear layers grows in proportion to the uncahced tokens of the batch, and that of the attention grows in proportion to its query–key pairs. Under causal attention, the ii-th uncached token attends to the tct_{\mathrm{c}} cached tokens and to the first ii uncached tokens, including itself. A request therefore computes A=tuc​tc+tuc​(tuc+1)/2A=t_{\mathrm{uc}}t_{\mathrm{c}}+t_{\mathrm{uc}}(t_{\mathrm{uc}}+1)/2 query–key pairs (5(b)). A request reuses its cached prefix from GPU memory or from host memory. Asynchronous fetches hide most of the restore from host memory (Section 4.2), but each restored token still adds a small cost to the iteration, such as the remaining host-to-GPU copy. This cost grows in proportion to the restored tokens. Each iteration also pays a fixed cost, such as the time to launch its kernels. A prefill iteration on node nn thus takes

TP,niter=cn,0+cn,1​∑tuc+cn,2​∑A+cn,3​∑trst,T^{\mathrm{iter}}_{\mathrm{P},n}=c_{n,0}+c_{n,1}\textstyle\sum t_{\mathrm{uc}}+c_{n,2}\textstyle\sum A+c_{n,3}\textstyle\sum t_{\mathrm{rst}}, (1)

where the sums run over the requests of the batch, and trstt_{\mathrm{rst}} is the number of tokens that a request restores from host memory. The coefficients cn,0c_{n,0} to cn,3c_{n,3} give the fixed cost of an iteration and the time per uncached token, per query–key pair, and per restored token. They depend on the model, hardware, and parallelism of node nn, and Evolving Infra fits them online, as described at the end of this section. Appendix B.2 shows that Equation (1) also holds for sliding-window, linear, and sparse attention, including the DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) of GLM-5.2.

Decode iteration-time model. Decode spends most of its time in memory-bound kernels [80], whose execution time grows in proportion to the bytes they read. Most of these bytes belong to the model weights. Each iteration reads the dense weights in full, which forms a fixed cost. In the mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, the iteration reads only the weights of the routed experts that its tokens select. A decode iteration serves the BB running requests of a node, and each request feeds tfwdt_{\mathrm{fwd}} tokens into the iteration, a number that exceeds one under speculative decoding. With each token selecting kk of the EE routed experts, the tfwd​Bt_{\mathrm{fwd}}B tokens select an expected fraction ϕ⁡(B)=1−(1−k/E)tfwd​B\phi(B)=1-(1-k/E)^{t_{\mathrm{fwd}}B} of them (Appendix B.3). A decode iteration holds only a few tokens, and this fraction therefore changes with BB. Each running request also adds about the same time to the iteration, for example to sample its next tokens and to draft tokens for speculative decoding. This part of the iteration time grows in proportion to BB. The time to read the KV of running requests also grows in proportion to their total context length. GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6, however, stores little KV per token and reads only part of it under sparse attention (Appendix B.4). At 8 or more running requests, the context length thus changes the iteration time by only 2–7% (5(d)), and the model omits this term. A decode iteration on node nn thus takes

TD,niter​(B)=dn,0+dn,1​ϕ​(B)+dn,2​B.T^{\mathrm{iter}}_{\mathrm{D},n}(B)=d_{n,0}+d_{n,1}\,\phi(B)+d_{n,2}\,B. (2)

The coefficients dn,0d_{n,0} to dn,2d_{n,2} give the fixed cost of an iteration, the time to read the weights of all routed experts, and the time per running request. Like the prefill coefficients, they depend on the model, hardware, and parallelism of node nn, and Evolving Infra fits them online.

Request time and node throughput. In Equation (1), every term except the fixed cost sums over the requests of the batch. A request thus occupies the prefill node for its own share of these terms plus part of the fixed cost, which we divide among the requests in proportion to their uncached tokens. With t¯n\bar{t}_{n} the average number of new tokens per prefill iteration on node nn and fnf_{n} the fraction of cached tokens that the node restores from host memory, a request with work ww occupies node nn for

TP,nreq​(w)=cn,0​tuc/t¯n+cn,1​tuc+cn,2​A+cn,3​fn​tcT^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{P},n}(w)=c_{n,0}\,t_{\mathrm{uc}}/\bar{t}_{n}+c_{n,1}\,t_{\mathrm{uc}}+c_{n,2}\,A+c_{n,3}\,f_{n}\,t_{\mathrm{c}} (3)

in prefill. In decode, each iteration advances every running request by tacct_{\mathrm{acc}} tokens on average, and a request needs tout/tacct_{\mathrm{out}}/t_{\mathrm{acc}} iterations to finish. Since the BB running requests share each iteration, a request occupies node nn for

TD,nreq​(w)=TD,niter​(B)​tout/(B​tacc)T^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{D},n}(w)=T^{\mathrm{iter}}_{\mathrm{D},n}(B)\,t_{\mathrm{out}}\big/\bigl(B\,t_{\mathrm{acc}}\bigr) (4)

in decode. Node nn thus completes μP,n=1/TP,nreq​(w)\mu_{\mathrm{P},n}=1/T^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{P},n}(w) requests per second in prefill and μD,n=1/TD,nreq​(w)\mu_{\mathrm{D},n}=1/T^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{D},n}(w) requests per second in decode.

Online fitting. Evolving Infra fits both models purely online at the start of serving. During a warmup period, every node serves both phases in a collocated mode, and Evolving Infra records the prefill and decode work that each node completes in fixed windows. It fits the coefficients of both models for each node by nonnegative least squares, freezes them, and then starts PD disaggregation from the initial split. After warmup, Evolving Infra periodically remeasures only t¯n\bar{t}_{n} and fnf_{n}, which change with the workload composition (2(b)). On controlled measurements on GB300, the model form predicts iteration time with a mean error below 7% outside the fitted settings (Figure 5).

5.2 Online phase-split adaptation

To size the PD split for diverse agent workloads and their shifting composition (2(a) and 2(b)), the planner reevaluates the possible splits by their predicted throughput at the end of each planning window of length TwinT_{\mathrm{win}}. Each request passes through both phases, and the slower phase thus determines the cluster throughput,

Θ⁡(𝒫,𝒟,w¯,q¯)=min⁡(∑n∈𝒫μP,n,∑n∈𝒟μD,n),\Theta(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{D};\bar{w},\bar{q})=\min\Bigl(\sum_{n\in\mathcal{P}}\mu_{\mathrm{P},n},\;\sum_{n\in\mathcal{D}}\mu_{\mathrm{D},n}\Bigr), (5)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒟\mathcal{D} together contain the NN nodes of the cluster. Here w¯\bar{w} is the average work of a request over the window, and q¯\bar{q} is the average number of requests in decode. Unlike queue depth, w¯\bar{w} characterizes the agent workload itself and barely changes during short bursts of sub-agents and forks. The planner evaluates μP,n\mu_{\mathrm{P},n} with w¯\bar{w} in Equation (3) and μD,n\mu_{\mathrm{D},n} with the batch B=q¯/|𝒟|B=\bar{q}/|\mathcal{D}| in TD,nreqT^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{D},n}.

Since each switch has a cost (Section 3.1), the planner switches only when another split is statistically better than the current one. For each prefill count other than the current one, the planner forms a candidate split (𝒫′,𝒟′)(\mathcal{P}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime}). It divides the window into mm slices and measures w¯i\bar{w}_{i} and q¯i\bar{q}_{i} on each slice ii. The gain of the candidate on slice ii is

gi=Θ⁡(𝒫′,𝒟′,w¯i,q¯i)−Θ⁡(𝒫,𝒟,w¯i,q¯i).g_{i}=\Theta(\mathcal{P}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime};\bar{w}_{i},\bar{q}_{i})-\Theta(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{D};\bar{w}_{i},\bar{q}_{i}). (6)

The candidate qualifies if its mean gain exceeds twice its standard error, g¯>2​σg/m\bar{g}>2\sigma_{g}/\sqrt{m}, where g¯\bar{g} and σg\sigma_{g} are the mean and standard deviation of the gains gig_{i}. This threshold keeps short bursts from triggering switches (Section 3.2). If any candidate qualifies, the planner switches to the one with the largest g¯\bar{g}. It applies the new split through the phase switch in Section 4.1, and Appendix E.3 summarizes the planner.

5.3 KV-reuse-aware eviction and routing

Eviction. The rules in Section 4.3 keep the count of a copy positive only while an active branch may still reuse it on that node. A block with a zero count, such as the history that compaction replaced, the context of a finished sub-agent, or the source copy left by a same-phase transfer (Figure 4), is thus KV that no active branch will reuse. Each node therefore evicts the blocks in its host memory in ascending order of the key (𝟙[Rb>0],Tb)(\mathds{1}[R_{b}>0],\,T_{b}), where RbR_{b} is the count of block bb on the node and TbT_{b} is its last access time. The node thus evicts zero-count blocks first, in LRU order, and evicts blocks with positive counts only after no zero-count block remains. Unlike LRU (Section 3.3), this order evicts replaced histories before the KV of branches that wait for tools, sub-agents, or users.

Routing. With asynchronous fetches (Section 4.2) and the eviction policy above, KV transfers are fast and memory-efficient. The router therefore balances the predicted TTFT across prefill nodes. For a request with work ww and prefill node nn, the router predicts

T^n​(w)=Tnrem+∑j∈QnTP,nreq​(wj)+TP,nreq​(w),\hat{T}_{n}(w)=T^{\mathrm{rem}}_{n}+\textstyle\sum_{j\in Q_{n}}T^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{P},n}(w_{j})+T^{\mathrm{req}}_{\mathrm{P},n}(w), (7)

where TnremT^{\mathrm{rem}}_{n} is the remaining time of the running batch on node nn, QnQ_{n} is the set of its queued requests, and each service time follows Equation (3). Appendix E.3 details how the prediction also charges the part of a fetch that outlasts the wait and the duplicate copy that the fetch creates. The router routes the request to the node with the smallest T^n​(w)\hat{T}_{n}(w), and that node fetches the KV of the request from the shared pool while the request waits. Unlike cache-aware routing (Section 3.3), this choice weighs the queue of each node against the KV that the node must fetch and avoids overloading nodes with popular prefixes.

6 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate Evolving Infra on coding, computer-use, and math agents served on 36 GB300 GPUs. Section 6.1 summarizes the setup. Section 6.2 evaluates each agent workload in isolation under a stationary load. Section 6.3 evaluates a shifting workload composition. Section 6.4 measures the sensitivity of Evolving Infra to the initial PD split, the contribution of each component, and the cost of online phase-split adaptation. Appendix D further evaluates Evolving Infra on up to 256 GPUs, in simulation at 3,072 GPUs, under open-loop arrivals, and with different parallelism for prefill and decode.

6.1 Experimental setup

Workloads. We deploy mini-SWE-agent [74] on PutnamBench [62, Putnam;] and Anthropic’s computer-use agent [5] on OSWorld 2.0 [77, OSWorld;]. Putnam is a decode-heavy workload that runs a single agent branch per problem without context management. OSWorld is a prefill-heavy, multimodal, multi-agent workload that appends a screenshot to the context at every step (2(a)). The Claude Code traces [51, CC;], collected from real users, form the most dynamic of the three workloads. They interleave sub-agents, compactions, and long pauses between requests (2(c)). Putnam and OSWorld thus differ most in their demand for prefill and decode, whereas CC exercises agent context management the most. We replay CC with the Trie replayer [8], which preserves the pauses between requests and the prefix sharing of the original traces. Trie fixes the length of each output and the duration of each tool call to their recorded values. Later requests carry these outputs and the recorded tool results, thereby preserving the prefix that each request shares with earlier requests.

Models and deployment. We serve GLM-5.2 [18] for Putnam and CC and Kimi K2.6 [26] for OSWorld and for the run with a shifting workload composition. Each model is quantized to NVFP4 with an FP8 KV cache and uses multi-token prediction (MTP) for speculative decoding. It runs with four-way tensor parallelism (TP4) on nine 4×\timesGB300 nodes [39]. On each node, host memory (L2) caches the KV of 4×\times as many tokens as GPU memory (L1).

Evaluation settings. Evolving Infra uses a planning window of Twin=600T_{\mathrm{win}}=600 s with m=10m=10 slices and learns its iteration-time models online (Section 5.1). Appendix E.3 lists the other parameters of our runs. Each run starts with a 30-minute warmup, which we exclude from measurement. After the warmup, stationary runs serve one agent workload for one hour at a fixed concurrency, replacing each finished agent with a new one. We test three concurrency levels per workload, namely 224, 256, and 288 agents for Putnam, 90, 108, and 126 for CC, and 128, 144, and 160 for OSWorld. The run with a shifting workload composition serves 288 concurrent Putnam agents, 144 Putnam and 72 OSWorld agents, and 144 OSWorld agents in three consecutive hours after the warmup, shifting demand toward prefill.

Baselines. We compare Evolving Infra with Dynamo v1.5.1 [40] in the configuration of Section 3. To our knowledge, Dynamo is the state-of-the-art open-source system for dynamic PD disaggregation. Both start from the prefill-heavy split 6P3D, a common assumption for agentic workloads [4]. For the shifting workload composition, the ablation (Section 6.4), and the lowest concurrency of each stationary workload (Appendix D.1), we also compare with the best static split, which runs SGLang PD disaggregation at the fixed split with the highest throughput over the whole run [48]. All baselines use the SGLang Model Gateway [58] with cache-aware prefill routing and round-robin decode routing, the setup with the lowest P95 TTFT in Section 3.3. Each node runs HiCache [72] with LRU eviction and the same deduplicated host memory as Evolving Infra (Appendix A.5). We do not compare with the runtime role switch of SGLang [53], because it rejects speculative decoding, which both models use. Llumnix [32] cannot run on the Arm CPUs of our GB300 nodes, and Appendix A.1 compares it with Evolving Infra on H200 GPUs.

6.2 Stationary workloads

Low-cost online adaptation across agent workloads. Evolving Infra outperforms Dynamo in throughput, lost KV reuse, and mean E2E latency for every agent workload (Figure 6). It achieves 1.10–2.73×\times the throughput of Dynamo (Appendix C.4), reduces lost KV reuse by 81–95%, and lowers the mean E2E latency by 1.15–4.12×\times and the P95 TTFT by up to 13.92×\times. At the lowest concurrency of each workload, it also achieves 0.98–1.38×\times the throughput of the best static split under SGLang (Appendix D.1). Averaged over all nine settings, a phase switch of Evolving Infra completes in 6.2 s, including the wait for the running requests of the node, which the node keeps serving. This is over 100×\times shorter than a Dynamo relaunch, which takes 754 s on average and keeps the node out of service throughout (Appendix C.1). The symmetric engine (Section 4.1) and the shared KV pool (Section 4.2) thus avoid the relaunch and retain the KV of the switching node, the two costs of a phase switch in Section 3.1. They stay fast when prefill and decode use different parallelism (Appendix D.4).

Accurate compute allocation for diverse agent workloads. Evolving Infra reduces the mean E2E latency by 3.80–4.12×\times on CC, 2.34–2.69×\times on OSWorld, and 1.15–1.23×\times on Putnam relative to Dynamo (middle row of Figure 6). The planner (Section 5.2) contributes to this gain by matching the PD split to the compute demand of each workload purely online. It selects 3P6D–4P5D for CC and 8P1D for OSWorld (Appendix C.2). These splits differ from the best static splits under SGLang in 2(a), 4P5D and 6P3D, since the symmetric engines shift the best split (Appendix D.1). On the decode-heavy Putnam, the planner keeps only one or two prefill nodes to maximize throughput. This choice trades P95 TTFT for throughput, raising the P95 TTFT above that of Dynamo at 224 and 288 agents while lowering the mean E2E latency. Unlike the coarse signals in Section 3.2, the iteration-time models separate cached from uncached tokens (Section 5.1), and the average work of a request barely changes during short bursts. Evolving Infra thus switches only 2.0 times per run on average, whereas the Dynamo planner reacts to queue depth and KV utilization, switches 3.6 times per run, and deviates from the best static split of each workload for 41–100% of the measurement period (Appendix C.2). Under open-loop arrivals, the planner also gives prefill more nodes as agents arrive faster, and Evolving Infra sustains twice the arrival rate of the best static split (Appendix D.3).

Accurate KV cache management under agent context management. Since asynchronous fetches make moving KV fast (Section 4.2), the router routes each request to the node with the shortest predicted TTFT (Section 5.3) rather than to the few nodes holding its prefix (Section 3.3). Evolving Infra thus reduces the P95 TTFT by 3.25–13.92×\times on CC and OSWorld relative to Dynamo (bottom row of Figure 6). On CC, the most loaded prefill node queues requests 1.75–1.85×\times as long as the average node, versus 2.29–2.61×\times under cache-aware routing (Appendix C.3). With the counts of the directory (Section 4.3), the eviction of Evolving Infra (Section 5.3) retains nearly all the KV that agents still need (top row of Figure 6). In contrast, the LRU eviction of Dynamo drops the KV of branches that wait for tools, sub-agents, or users, which accounts for 34–46% of its lost KV reuse on CC. The fraction of prompt tokens that Dynamo prefills without cached KV is up to 2.99×\times that of Evolving Infra (Appendix C.1).

6.3 Shifting workload composition

Precise and timely adaptation to a shifting workload composition. The PD split of Evolving Infra tracks the best split of each 10-minute window as the planner (Section 5.2) follows the shift from Putnam to OSWorld (7(a)). In the OSWorld period, it settles at 8P1D, one prefill node more than the best split under SGLang, since the symmetric engines shift the best split (Appendix D.1). The best static split balances prefill and decode only in the mixed period (2(b)). The Dynamo planner keeps fewer prefill nodes than the best split for most of the run, as Section 3.2 predicts. Evolving Infra thus reduces the mean E2E latency by 2.15×\times and 1.33×\times and the P95 TTFT by 3.58×\times and 1.88×\times relative to Dynamo and the best static split, respectively (Figure 7b, c). It also achieves 2.14×\times the throughput of Dynamo and 1.28×\times that of the best static split, and the highest throughput in every period (Appendix C.4).

6.4 Ablation study

Sensitivity to the initial PD split. Evolving Infra achieves a similar mean E2E latency from every initial split (8(a)). Serving CC with 126 concurrent agents from four initial splits, from 3P6D to 6P3D, its mean E2E latency varies by at most 1.8%. In all four runs, the planner converges to 4P5D (Appendix C.2). On this workload, online phase-split adaptation thus does not need a well-chosen initial split.

Contribution of each component. On CC with 126 concurrent agents, the infrastructure of Section 4 and the KV-reuse-aware eviction and routing of Section 5.3 alone achieve 1.37×\times the throughput of the best static split at the same 4P5D split, without online phase-split adaptation (8(b)). With the routing of SGLang, asynchronous KV fetching alone achieves 1.12×\times the throughput of upstream SGLang, because it cuts the idle time of prefill nodes from 23.6% to 14.4% (Appendix D.6). KV-reuse-aware routing and eviction contribute the rest. Compared with cache-aware routing at the same split, Evolving Infra loses 0.7% instead of 2.4% of the KV reuse and prefills 31% fewer uncached prompt tokens per request (Appendix D.5). Pausing agents as ThunderAgent does brings no such gain (0.95×\times), because KV capacity does not limit serving on GB300 nodes (Appendix D.5).

Cost of online phase-split adaptation. Enabling online phase-split adaptation at the best static split lowers the throughput by only 0.3% (8(b)). Online adaptation thus costs almost no throughput even when the initial split is already the best. It also avoids offline profiling, which takes 10,752 GPU-hours for the three-hour CC trace on 256 GPUs even with a binary search and recurs for every agent workload (Appendix D.2). Online fitting is fast as well. The iteration-time models converge to a low mean error within a minute of learning (8(c)), far shorter than the 30-minute warmup of our runs.

7 Conclusions

We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that decouples compute allocation from KV cache management. Existing PD-disaggregated systems tie the KV cache of each node to the phase of that node. Changing the PD split thus either relaunches a node or loses its KV. Keeping KV on its node also forces routing to trade load balance against cache locality. In Evolving Infra, symmetric engines switch the phase of a node in place. A shared KV pool keeps the KV of every node readable by all other nodes.

On this data plane, Evolving Infra adapts compute allocation to diverse agent workloads and their shifting composition, and KV cache management to agent context management. Its planner reassigns nodes between prefill and decode with iteration-time models that separate cached from uncached tokens and are fitted online. Its router balances predicted TTFT across prefill nodes. With the branch counts of the KV directory, each node evicts first the KV that no active branch references, such as replaced histories and the contexts of finished sub-agents.

On 36 GB300 GPUs, a phase switch of Evolving Infra takes 6.2 s on average, over 100×\times shorter than a Dynamo relaunch. Under stationary load, Evolving Infra delivers up to 2.73×\times the throughput of Dynamo, loses 81–95% less KV reuse, and reduces the mean E2E latency by up to 4.12×\times. Under a shifting workload composition, it reduces the mean E2E latency by 2.15×\times and 1.33×\times relative to Dynamo and the best static split, respectively. These gains hold on 256 GB300 GPUs and, in simulation, on 3,072 GPUs (Appendix D.2).
