Appendix A Additional Related Work

This appendix extends the review of Section 2.2. Appendix A.1 details how existing systems change the PD split. Appendix A.2 and Appendix A.3 describe the KV tiers and the KV index that Sections 4.2 and 4.3 build on. Appendix A.4 compares agent-aware KV management with Evolving Infra, and Appendix A.5 explains why host memory can hold the KV that agents reuse.

A.1 Prefill–decode split adaptation

Current serving engines fix their phase at launch by default. Systems that adapt the PD split around this limit either relaunch engines, which takes minutes and empties their KV caches, or switch them in place. Those that switch in place lose the KV of a switched engine or size the pools with a coarse cost model. Others keep the roles of nodes fixed and shift only compute or KV between the phases, inside an engine or between fixed prefill and decode nodes.

vLLM and SGLang relaunch to change phase.

In SGLang, a flag at launch makes each engine a prefill or a decode engine, and the router is given separate lists of prefill and decode engines [54]. The two roles run different scheduling loops with role-specific state. A prefill engine keeps a bootstrap queue and sends KV to decode engines. A decode engine reserves KV slots for each incoming request before its prefill finishes, receives KV through its own threads and queues, and captures CUDA graphs for decoding [54, 53]. vLLM likewise configures each engine at launch to produce KV for prefill or to consume it for decode, and its proxy is given fixed lists of prefill and decode engines [64]. Changing the phase of an engine thus requires relaunching it with a new configuration. SGLang’s recent opt-in runtime switch avoids the relaunch, but it still drains the engine to idle and releases its prefix cache [53]. Systems built on these engines therefore relaunch them. The Dynamo planner changes the phase of a node by terminating its worker, without waiting for in-flight requests, and launching a worker of the other phase [42]. The new worker must load the model and starts with an empty KV cache, and Dynamo notes that spinning up a GPU worker takes minutes [42]. In the runs of Section 6.2, a Dynamo switch takes 754 s on average, from the planner decision until the relaunched worker is ready, and on CC with 108 agents Dynamo loses 4.9% of the available KV reuse over its four switches (Appendix C.1). While a node relaunches, only eight of the nine nodes serve requests, which covers 44–91% of the one-hour measurement period (Appendix C.2).

Arrow switches in place but loses KV.

Arrow [69] keeps nodes stateless, so that any node can serve both prefill and decode requests, and it moves nodes between the prefill and decode pools without a restart. Its code is not public, so Section 3 evaluates our reimplementation of its planner and scheduler on the symmetric engines of Evolving Infra. Arrow has three problems on agentic workloads. It sizes the pools by TTFT and TPOT, which agent context management makes fluctuate. It predicts TTFT from the full input length, which ignores KV reuse. Its scheduler also ignores where KV is cached, and each node keeps its KV in its own cache, so later prefills do not reuse the KV of a node that moves to the decode pool. In our runs on CC, Arrow switches nodes 34 times, ends at 8P1D, and delivers 65% less throughput than the best static split under SGLang PD disaggregation (Section 3.2). In these runs, it loses 55.5% of the available KV reuse (Section 3.1).

xLLM cannot switch phases and route by cached KV at once.

xLLM [31] switches nodes between phases in place, but its open-source service implements this switching and KV-aware routing as alternative policies chosen at launch [73]. Only its SLO-aware policy switches phases, and it flips single nodes in reaction to individual requests instead of sizing the split with a planner. This policy predicts TTFT from the full prompt length, so it counts cached prefixes as prefill work and ignores where KV is cached. Its cache-aware policy routes by prefix hits but never switches phases.

Llumnix adapts the split with a coarse cost model.

Llumnix [60] reschedules running requests across engines by live-migrating each request together with its KV, which balances load, reduces memory fragmentation, and isolates high-priority requests. Its adaptive PD mode assigns phases to engines at runtime to meet TTFT and TPOT targets [32], using a cost model that predicts TTFT by interpolating between profiled points by the number of prefill tokens and the decode load [33]. A single token count cannot separate the uncached tokens of an agent request from the long cached prefix they attend to. Part of its KV transfer stack is also released only as a pre-built binary without source code, so we could not run Llumnix on the Arm CPUs of our GB300 nodes. In our runs on H200 GPUs, Llumnix delivers 12.2% less throughput than the best static split (Figure A.1).

semi-PD shares KV between the phases only inside an engine.

semi-PD [19] runs a prefill process and a decode process on every GPU of an engine, divides the SMs of each GPU between them through NVIDIA MPS, and keeps one copy of the weights and the KV, its unified storage, in the GPU memory of the engine. Shifting SMs restarts only these processes, while a resident process keeps the weights and the KV, so semi-PD avoids costly phase switches inside an engine. Its controller, however, shifts SMs to the phase whose TTFT or TPOT misses its target, and the prefill bursts of agents, such as sub-agents that start together, perturb both (Section 3.2). Across engines, its router weighs the KV cache hit rate of each engine against GPU utilization and queue depth, the trade-off between cache locality and load balance of Section 3.3.

MemServe and PPD reuse multi-turn KV but keep the split fixed.

MemServe [20] and PPD [28] let the later turns of a conversation reuse the KV that its previous turn left on the decode side. MemServe moves this KV to the prefill engine: the decode engine sends the KV that it produced back after each request, and a global scheduler routes each request by where its prefix is cached. PPD instead moves the prefill to the KV: it prefills the uncached tokens of a later turn on the decode node that holds the KV of the conversation, which slows decoding far less than a full prefill does, and a table profiled offline decides per request whether to take this path. Neither, however, adapts the split: MemServe’s engines are prefill-only, decode-only, or colocated, and PPD restarts its engines to change the split, so neither follows the shifting workload composition (2(b)). PPD’s offline table, as its authors note, becomes suboptimal when the workload drifts far from the one it was profiled on. MemServe also judges KV reuse from stale records: its scheduler learns where KV resides only from the responses that pass through it, so it misses evictions and expires its records after a fixed time-to-live. PPD keeps the KV of a conversation on one decode node, so each later turn either runs on that node or recomputes the previous response on a prefill node.

Evolving Infra instead switches the phase of a node in place, and the shared KV pool keeps the KV of the node readable by all other nodes (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

A.2 KV memory hierarchy in current serving engines

Section 4.2builds the shared KV pool of Evolving Infra on SGLang HiCache. This subsection describes how current engines tier KV, how they share it across nodes through Mooncake, and why this sharing adds latency.

Private host tiers.

SGLang HiCache backs the GPU KV cache (L1) of an engine with host memory (L2) and an optional storage backend (L3) such as Mooncake Store [72, 52]. L1 and L2 are private to each engine, and every tensor-parallel rank allocates its own L2 pool. Engines therefore never read each other’s L2: KV that one engine computes becomes visible to another only after it reaches L3 [52].

Sharing through Mooncake.

Mooncake Store pools the DRAM that nodes contribute into a cluster-wide object store. A master service keeps the metadata of each object, and clients move the data directly over RDMA with the Mooncake Transfer Engine [35, 36]. A put first asks the master to allocate space and then commits the object, and a get first asks the master where the object is stored. SGLang backs up pages from L2 to Mooncake in the background, keyed by a hash of the prefix that ends at each page. When a request is queued, an engine asks Mooncake which pages of its prefix exist, prefetches them into its own L2, and loads them into GPU memory layer by layer during prefill [52, 57]. vLLM’s Mooncake store connector instead registers GPU memory with Mooncake and moves KV blocks directly between GPU memory and the pool [49], and a newer SGLang option links its radix cache to Mooncake in the same way, without HiCache’s host tier [57].

Why fetching through the pool adds latency.

KV takes extra hops. With HiCache, it moves from the L2 of the producing engine into a Mooncake segment, which may lie on a third node, and from there into the L2 of the consuming engine before it reaches the GPU. Every lookup, put, and get also involves RPCs to the master, and a page becomes visible only after its backup commits [35]. The prefetch starts when the request is queued but fills only L2, and the GPU loads the pages layer by layer during prefill. If the prefetch has not finished when the prefill could start, SGLang stops it under the best-effort policy and recomputes the pages that have not arrived, waits for it under the wait-complete policy, and under the default timeout policy waits until a deadline and then recomputes the rest [52, 57]. Mooncake’s own benchmark accordingly finds HiCache slightly faster with L2 alone than with Mooncake at equal hit rates in its first rounds, because L2 alone avoids fetching from remote storage [37]. The same KV can also occupy the L2 of the producer, the pool, and the L2 of each consumer at once. Evolving Infra instead lets prefill nodes read KV directly from the L2 of any peer over RDMA, restores it into GPU memory before the prefill begins, and keeps L2 across phase switches (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

A.3 Dynamo KV indexer and router

The KV directory of Evolving Infra (Section 4.3) follows the KV indexer of the Dynamo router. This subsection describes how the index is built and updated, how the router scores nodes with it, and what it does not record.

Cluster-wide KV index.

The KV router of Dynamo keeps a cluster-wide index of cached KV in a prefix tree [44]. Each entry of the tree stands for one KV block, keyed by a hash of its tokens, and records the nodes that hold the block. To route a request, the router walks the tree along the blocks of the request and finds, for every node, how many leading blocks it already holds.

KV events.

Engines keep the tree current through KV events. SGLang and vLLM publish an event over ZMQ whenever they store or evict blocks, and a publisher on each node relays the events to the routers [43]. The engine identifies each block by a prefix hash over all tokens up to and including the block. When it stores new blocks, its event carries their tokens and prefix hashes and the prefix hash of their parent block. Through a per-node table from prefix hashes to tree entries, the router finds the entry of the parent block, descends from it along the token hashes of the new blocks, creating entries as needed, and adds the node to each of these entries [43, 44, 40]. When the engine evicts blocks, its event names them by their prefix hashes, and the router removes the node from their entries. With HiCache, SGLang also names the memory tier in each event, and the router tracks host memory and disk in separate indexes beside the GPU tree [41, 40].

Scoring.

For each candidate node, the router adds the prompt blocks of the request to the prefill blocks already assigned to the node, subtracts a credit for each leading block that the node already holds, and adds the blocks that the node would be decoding. The router tracks these loads itself from the requests that it routes, not from KV events, and sends the request to the node with the lowest cost [44]. A block held in GPU memory earns a full credit, while blocks in host memory and on disk earn 0.75 and 0.25 by default [41]. The host and disk credits are constants: they depend neither on how long loading the blocks takes nor on the running requests that the loading delays on the node. Evolving Infra instead predicts the TTFT of the request on each prefill node, including the part of a KV fetch that the wait in the queue does not hide (Section 5.3 and Appendix E.3).

What the index does not record.

The index records where each block is cached, on which nodes and in which tier, but not which requests or agent branches will reuse it. KV events report only stores and evictions, not the forks, compactions, and finished sub-agents that decide this reuse. Eviction therefore stays with each engine, and SGLang evicts in LRU order by default [55]. Dynamo can also pass a per-request priority from the harness to SGLang, which can then evict the KV of the lowest-priority requests first [46]. Neither recency nor priority changes when compaction replaces a history or a KV transfer leaves a copy behind: these blocks keep their last access time, and a cached prefix keeps the highest priority among the requests that reached it [55]. Evolving Infra keeps the same event-driven tree and adds one attribute to each block, the number of active branches that reference it on each node (Section 4.3). The counts follow agent context management and KV transfers, and each node evicts the host-memory blocks with zero counts first (Section 5.3).

A.4 Agent-aware KV management and routers

This subsection compares Evolving Infra with systems that use the structure of agents to manage KV.

Program-aware scheduling.

ThunderAgent [23] and Continuum [27] schedule the requests of an agent together so that its KV survives tool calls. Continuum pins the KV of a multi-turn program in GPU memory for a time-to-live that it estimates from the durations of past calls to the same tool. ThunderAgent abstracts each agent workflow as a program. When the programs on a data-parallel replica need more KV than its GPU cache holds, ThunderAgent pauses programs that wait for tools, evicts their KV, and resumes them later, possibly on another replica with free memory. Both systems thus target KV-cache thrashing, in which the KV of a waiting program is evicted from GPU memory and its whole context must be prefilled again. Both run prefill and decode on the same nodes, and both treat the context of a program as growing only by appending.

Thrashing on current models and hardware.

Thrashing occurs only when programs need more KV than a replica can hold. Current engines back GPU memory with a host-memory tier, and compact KV representations together with deduplication let this tier hold several times as much KV as GPU memory (Appendix A.5). A context evicted from GPU memory then stays in host memory and is reloaded rather than recomputed. ThunderAgent found such offloading too slow over PCIe [23], but on GB300 nodes the reload runs over the NVLink-C2C link between the Grace CPUs and the GPUs [39, 10]. In our runs, Dynamo, whose SGLang engines evict host memory in LRU order, loses at most 7.8% of the available KV reuse, and Evolving Infra at most 1.0%, without pausing any agent (Appendix C.1). Host memory instead keeps KV that no active branch needs: the source copies that KV transfers leave, the histories that compaction replaces, and the contexts of finished sub-agents. Evolving Infra therefore counts the branches that reference each copy (Section 4.3) instead of pausing agents. Appendix D.5 compares Evolving Infra with ThunderAgent and cache-aware routing on GB300 nodes.

Agent-aware KV management.

KVTether [17] exports runtime context operations from agent harnesses and maps them to KV lifecycle states, accounting for shared prefixes across contexts. These states guide cache admission, reclamation, and eviction in a multi-tier cache with cross-node transfers. Its presented design focuses on KV lifecycle management and does not address online adaptation of the PD split; its evaluation uses a fixed PD configuration.

A.5 Extending host memory with deduplication

Section 4.2keeps the KV that agents reuse in host memory (L2), and Appendix A.4 argues that this tier largely absorbs KV thrashing. This subsection explains why L2 is large enough.

Compact KV.

Although smaller than L3, L2 is sufficient for recent open models [18, 25]. These models increasingly adopt compact KV representations such as MQA [59] and MLA [12]. In MLA, all attention heads share one latent vector of 576 values per token and layer. With an FP8 KV cache, a token takes about 35 KB of KV in Kimi K2.6 and about 50 KB in GLM-5.2, including the keys of the sparse-attention indexer of GLM-5.2. Full multi-head attention at the same precision would need 36×\times and about 50×\times as much.

Deduplication across tensor-parallel ranks.

Because all heads share the latent vector, tensor parallelism does not split MLA KV: every rank holds the complete KV of each token [52]. SGLang HiCache allocates its host pool per rank and thus stores the same KV once per GPU in L2, although only one rank writes it to the storage backend [52]. vLLM’s CPU offloading instead keeps one copy of each replicated MLA block in a host region that all ranks share, so that at a tensor-parallel degree of NN the host tier holds about NN times as many blocks [63]. LMCache saves MLA KV from one rank and broadcasts it to the other ranks on retrieval [34]. Our engines deduplicate L2 in the same way: L2 stores a single copy per node for all attention heads and broadcasts it to all GPUs of the node when fetched in L1. All systems in our evaluation, including the baselines, use this deduplication. When serving GLM-5.2 on NVIDIA GB300, L2 typically holds 4×\times as much KV as L1. A GB300 node has about 1 TB of host memory [39], which could hold about 20 million tokens of GLM-5.2 KV as a single copy, but only about 5 million if each of its four GPUs kept its own copy.

Production traces of a large cloud provider show that the cache size needed for an ideal hit ratio is moderate [66]. With a deduplicated host tier, capacity thus rarely forces recomputation in our runs (Appendix A.4), and the remaining waste lies in KV that no active branch references (Section 4.3).

Appendix B Extended Theoretical Analysis

This appendix extends the iteration-time models of Section 5.1. Appendix B.1 fits both models on another GPU and model. Appendix B.2 explains why the prefill iteration-time model holds for attention architectures other than full attention. Appendix B.3 derives ϕ⁡(B)\phi(B), the fraction of routed experts that a decode iteration reads, and Appendix B.4 explains why the decode iteration-time model omits the context length.

B.1 Iteration-time models on H200 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash

We repeat the measurement of Figure 5 on a second GPU and model to test whether the form of the iteration-time models holds beyond GB300 and GLM-5.2. The engine serves DeepSeek-V4-Flash [15] on four H200 GPUs with four-way tensor parallelism (TP4). DeepSeek-V4-Flash differs from GLM-5.2 in the two components that shape the models, attention and the MoE layers. Its attention combines a sliding window with compressed attention (Appendix B.2), and its MoE layers route each token to 6 of 256 experts instead of 8 of 256. Its speculative decoding feeds tfwd=6t_{\mathrm{fwd}}=6 tokens of each running request into every decode iteration. We measure the same settings as in Figure 5. As there, we fit the prefill model on 20 single-request settings and the decode model on the ten points with a 16K context.

Figure B.1shows that both models track the measured iteration times as closely as on GB300. Outside the 20 fitted settings, the prefill model has a mean error of 2.6% on the 28 single-request settings and 1.9% on the 12 batches of 2–8 requests. No batch deviates by more than 4.1%, including the batches of eight requests at a 256K cached prefix. Outside the ten fitted points, the decode model has a mean error of 3.6%.

B.2 Prefill iteration-time model beyond full attention

Under full attention, each uncached token attends to all cached tokens and to the uncached tokens before it. A request with tct_{\mathrm{c}} cached tokens and tuct_{\mathrm{uc}} uncached tokens thus computes A=tuc​tc+tuc​(tuc+1)/2A=t_{\mathrm{uc}}t_{\mathrm{c}}+t_{\mathrm{uc}}(t_{\mathrm{uc}}+1)/2 query–key pairs (Section 5.1). Many current models let an uncached token attend to only part of the earlier tokens. This subsection explains how these attention layers work and why the prefill iteration-time model in Equation (1) still expresses their time.

Sliding-window attention.

A sliding window lets each token attend only to a fixed number of the most recent tokens [11, 21]. Once the context is longer than the window, every uncached token computes the same number of query–key pairs, independent of tct_{\mathrm{c}}. The attention time of a request thus grows in proportion to tuct_{\mathrm{uc}}, and the term cn,1​∑tucc_{n,1}\sum t_{\mathrm{uc}} in Equation (1) captures it.

Linear attention.

Linear attention replaces the query–key pairs with earlier tokens by a state of fixed size [24, 75]. Each uncached token updates this state and computes its output from it, and the kernels process the uncached tokens in chunks of a fixed length. Every uncached token thus costs the same, independent of tct_{\mathrm{c}}. The attention time of a request grows in proportion to tuct_{\mathrm{uc}}, and the term cn,1​∑tucc_{n,1}\sum t_{\mathrm{uc}} in Equation (1) captures it.

DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA).

DSA, which GLM-5.2 uses [14, 18], splits attention into two steps. A lightweight indexer first scores every earlier token of each uncached token, and the core attention then attends only to the 2048 tokens with the highest scores. Each score is one query–key pair, and the indexer thus computes AA pairs per request, as full attention does, at a lower cost per pair. Its time grows with AA, and the term cn,2​∑Ac_{n,2}\sum A in Equation (1) captures it. The core attention computes at most 2048 pairs per uncached token, and its time grows with tuct_{\mathrm{uc}}, which the term cn,1​∑tucc_{n,1}\sum t_{\mathrm{uc}} captures.

Compressed attention in DeepSeek-V4.

Most layers of DeepSeek-V4 [15] combine a sliding window of 128 tokens with one of two compressed attentions. Both compress the keys and values of consecutive tokens into entries, and an uncached token attends to these entries instead of the tokens. Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) builds one entry per 4 tokens. Like DSA, its indexer scores all earlier entries, and its core attention attends to the 512 entries with the highest scores. Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) builds one entry per 128 tokens and attends to all earlier entries. DeepSeek-V4-Flash alternates CSA and HCA in 41 of its 43 layers and uses the sliding window alone in the other two. The CSA indexer and HCA compute one pair per 4 and per 128 earlier tokens, about A/4A/4 and A/128A/128 pairs per request, and their time grows with AA. The sliding window, the CSA core attention, and the compression take a fixed time per uncached token, and their time per request thus grows with tuct_{\mathrm{uc}}. The terms cn,2​∑Ac_{n,2}\sum A and cn,1​∑tucc_{n,1}\sum t_{\mathrm{uc}} in Equation (1) thus capture both parts.

B.3 MoE weights in the decode iteration-time model

In an MoE model, a decode iteration reads the dense weights in full but reads a routed expert only when some token selects it. The dense weights, such as the attention projections and the shared experts, serve every token, and reading them is part of the fixed cost dn,0d_{n,0} in Equation (2). In each MoE layer, a gate assigns every token to kk of the EE routed experts. The layer then reads the weights of each selected expert from GPU memory once and applies them to all tokens that select this expert. It does not read the weights of experts that no token selects. Our engines split every expert across the GPUs of a node with tensor parallelism, and each GPU reads its share of every selected expert. The time to read the routed experts thus grows in proportion to the number of selected experts. Equation (2) writes this time as dn,1​ϕ​(B)d_{n,1}\phi(B), where dn,1d_{n,1} is the time to read all routed experts and ϕ⁡(B)\phi(B) is the fraction that the iteration selects.

We derive ϕ⁡(B)\phi(B) under two assumptions. First, every expert receives the same share of tokens. MoE models are trained to keep the load of their experts balanced [13], and each token thus selects a given expert with probability k/Ek/E. Second, different tokens select their experts independently. Each of the BB running requests feeds tfwdt_{\mathrm{fwd}} tokens into every MoE layer, and the layer thus routes tfwd​Bt_{\mathrm{fwd}}B tokens. The probability that none of them selects a given expert is (1−k/E)tfwd​B(1-k/E)^{t_{\mathrm{fwd}}B}. The expected fraction of selected experts is one minus this probability, which gives ϕ⁡(B)=1−(1−k/E)tfwd​B\phi(B)=1-(1-k/E)^{t_{\mathrm{fwd}}B} in Section 5.1.

B.4 Context length in the decode iteration-time model

The decode iteration-time model omits the KV that an iteration reads for its running requests. This KV grows with their total context but stays small next to the weights that the iteration reads, for two reasons. First, recent models store little KV per token. With MLA, a token of GLM-5.2 takes about 50 KB of KV in FP8, about 50×\times less than under full multi-head attention (Appendix A.5). Second, sparse attention lets decode read only part of this KV. GLM-5.2 reads the full KV of at most 2048 selected tokens per layer and only the small indexer keys of all other tokens. DeepSeek-V4-Flash reads the full KV of its 128-token window and 512 selected entries, and of all other tokens only compressed entries or indexer keys that each cover 4 or 128 tokens (Appendix B.2). As a result, one million more context tokens lengthen a decode iteration by about 1 ms for GLM-5.2 on GB300 and by at most 1.5 ms for DeepSeek-V4-Flash on H200, whereas an iteration with 8 to 64 running requests takes 17 to 45 ms (5(d) and 1(d)).

Appendix C Extended Analysis of Stationary Workloads and the Shifting Workload Composition

This appendix explains the gains of Evolving Infra on the stationary workloads of Section 6.2 and under the shifting workload composition of Section 6.3. For the stationary workloads, Appendix C.1 compares the phase switches and KV reuse of Evolving Infra and Dynamo, Appendix C.2 shows how the PD split of each system changes over time, Appendix C.3 compares how evenly they balance prefill load, and Appendix C.4 relates their throughput to their E2E latency. For the shifting workload composition, Appendix C.4 also compares the throughput of Evolving Infra, Dynamo, and the best static split in each period. The Dynamo baseline in Section 6 and Appendices C and D corresponds to release v1.5.1 [40].

C.1 Phase Switches and KV Reuse

Table C.1lists, for every setting of Figure 6, the phase switches of each system in the measurement period, the mean time per switch, and the lost KV reuse. For Dynamo, the switch time runs from the planner decision to the point at which the relaunched engine is ready. For Evolving Infra, it runs from the planner decision to the point at which the node serves requests of its new phase, including the time to drain the requests running on the node. A phase switch of Evolving Infra takes 6.2 s on average, over 100×\times shorter than the 754 s that Dynamo needs to relaunch an engine, and retains the KV of the switching node. Evolving Infra thus loses 81–95% less KV reuse than Dynamo in every setting, even on Putnam, where it switches more often. As a result, the fraction of prompt tokens that Dynamo prefills without cached KV, one minus its KV hit rate in Table C.1, is 1.29–2.99×\times that of Evolving Infra.

On CC, the KV reuse that Dynamo loses has two main causes (Section 3.3). We attribute a loss to eviction when the request runs on the same prefill node as the previous request in its branch, and to routing when it runs on a different one. Eviction accounts for 39%, 34%, and 46% of the lost KV reuse with 90, 108, and 126 agents, because LRU eviction removes the KV of branches that pause for tools, sub-agents, or users. Routing accounts for another 22%, 17%, and 15%.

C.2 PD Split over Time

Figure C.1shows the PD split of both systems over the run for one setting of each agent workload. Evolving Infra changes its split at the first planner decision after warmup. It moves OSWorld to 8P1D and holds this split, moves CC to 3P6D and later to 4P5D, and alternates between 1P8D and 2P7D on Putnam. On OSWorld and CC, 8P1D and 3P6D are the best static splits on the symmetric engines of Evolving Infra (Appendix D.1). Dynamo changes its split by one node per relaunch. Each relaunch takes 10–15 minutes, during which only eight nodes serve requests, and these relaunches cover 44–91% of the measurement period, depending on the setting. Across all nine settings of Figure 6, Dynamo deviates from the best static split of each workload under SGLang PD disaggregation for 41–100% of the measurement period.

C.3 Prefill Load Balance

Table C.2reports the mean time that a prefill request waits in the queue of a prefill node and, as a measure of load balance, the queueing time on the most loaded prefill node relative to the average across prefill nodes, computed per minute and averaged over the measurement period. On CC, Evolving Infra keeps this ratio at 1.75–1.85×\times, compared with 2.29–2.61×\times under Dynamo, and reduces the queueing time by 2.6–7.6×\times.

C.4 Throughput and End-to-End Latency

The stationary runs serve a fixed number of agents in a closed loop (Section 6.1). A branch issues its next request only after its previous request completes and the pause between the two requests ends, during which the branch waits for tools, sub-agents, or users. By Little’s law [29], the throughput XX of a system satisfies

X=N¯branchT¯E2E+T¯pause,X=\frac{\bar{N}_{\mathrm{branch}}}{\bar{T}_{\mathrm{E2E}}+\bar{T}_{\mathrm{pause}}}, (C.1)

where N¯branch\bar{N}_{\mathrm{branch}} is the mean number of requests in flight plus the mean number of branches in a pause, T¯E2E\bar{T}_{\mathrm{E2E}} is the mean E2E latency, and T¯pause\bar{T}_{\mathrm{pause}} is the total pause time divided by the number of requests. In each setting, the two systems keep a similar N¯branch\bar{N}_{\mathrm{branch}}, for example 159 and 161 on CC with 126 concurrent agents. The lower T¯E2E\bar{T}_{\mathrm{E2E}} of Evolving Infra therefore translates into a higher throughput (Table C.3).

Within each period, the run with a shifting workload composition (Section 6.3) also serves a fixed number of agents in a closed loop, so Equation (C.1) holds for this run as well. Over the whole run, Evolving Infra reduces the mean E2E latency by 2.15×\times and 1.33×\times relative to Dynamo and the best static split, respectively (7(b)), and therefore achieves 2.14×\times the throughput of Dynamo and 1.28×\times that of the best static split (Table C.4). Its throughput is also the highest in every period.

Appendix D Additional Experiments

Beyond the settings of Section 6, we evaluate Evolving Infra under larger and more diverse deployments. Evolving Infra keeps its gain on 256 GB300 GPUs and, in simulation, on 3,072 GB300 GPUs (Appendix D.2), sustains twice the agent arrival rate of static 4P5D under open-loop arrivals (Appendix D.3), and remains effective when prefill and decode use different parallelism (Appendix D.4). Moreover, Evolving Infra outperforms ThunderAgent, an agent-aware router, since KV capacity does not limit serving on GB300 nodes (Appendix D.5), and its asynchronous KV fetching achieves 1.12×\times the throughput of upstream SGLang (Appendix D.6). Appendix D.1 explains why its best static split differs from that under SGLang PD disaggregation.

D.1 Best Static Split on the Symmetric Engines

The best static split of Section 6.1 is profiled offline under SGLang PD disaggregation (Figure 2). Evolving Infra serves requests on its symmetric engines (Section 4.1), so its best static split may differ. This subsection compares the best static split of Evolving Infra with that of SGLang on the stationary workloads of Section 6.2.

Experimental Setup.

We serve Putnam, CC, and OSWorld with 224, 90, and 128 concurrent agents, the lowest concurrency level of each agent workload in Section 6.2. As in Section 6.1, we serve GLM-5.2 for Putnam and CC and Kimi K2.6 for OSWorld on 36 GB300 GPUs. SGLang runs in its PD disaggregation mode at its best static split in 2(a), with the router and HiCache settings of our baselines (Section 6.1). Evolving Infra runs at its best static split, with online phase-split adaptation disabled and its PD split fixed for the whole run. We score minutes 30 to 85 of each run, and each configuration runs once.

Results.

The symmetric engines shift the best static split from 4P5D to 3P6D for CC and from 6P3D to 8P1D for OSWorld (Table D.1). For Putnam, 2P7D is the best static split on both systems. The shift is largest for OSWorld and stems from how the two systems allocate the GPU memory of decode nodes. SGLang reserves GPU memory on a decode node for the KV of each request before its prefill begins. It holds this reservation while the request waits in the queue of a prefill node. At 6P3D, these reservations occupy 91% of the KV cache of its three decode nodes on average, so removing a decode node would delay prefill. Evolving Infra instead selects the decode node of a request only when its prefill begins, so queued requests occupy no memory on decode nodes. With a single decode node, the mean E2E latency of OSWorld exceeds its mean TTFT by only 2.6 s (24.2 s versus 21.6 s). Evolving Infra therefore assigns the remaining eight nodes to prefill. With online phase-split adaptation, Evolving Infra reaches 8.81, 5.40, and 4.30 requests/s in these settings (Table C.3), 0.98–1.38×\times the throughput of the best static split under SGLang.

D.2 Scaling to Larger Clusters

This subsection evaluates Evolving Infra on real clusters of up to 256 GB300 GPUs and on a simulated cluster of 3,072 GPUs. Both show that the aggregate PD demand varies less as the cluster grows, whereas the imbalance within the cluster grows.

Setup on up to 256 GPUs.

We serve the Claude Code traces with GLM-5.2 on 36, 64, 128, and 256 GB300 GPUs and scale the number of concurrent agents with the GPUs, 10 agents per GPU. Static PD runs SGLang in its PD disaggregation mode at a fixed split, with the router and HiCache settings of Section 6.1.

The aggregate split matters less at scale.

On 256 GPUs, static PD keeps 81–103% of the throughput of 24P40D across P/D ratios from 0.33 to 1.29 (Figure D.1a). The demand of many agents together varies less over time, and each node holds a smaller fraction of the capacity. A mismatch between the split and the aggregate demand thus costs less throughput than on 36 GPUs.

The imbalance among nodes grows.

The P95 TTFT of static PD, however, rises about threefold from 36 to 256 GPUs, from 142 s to 418 s (Figure D.1b). With more prefill nodes, the cache-aware router concentrates the requests of more agents on the few nodes that hold their prefixes. The router and the shared KV pool of Evolving Infra spread this load across nodes. Its P95 TTFT thus stays within 10–14 s, and its mean E2E latency rises by only 16% (Figure D.1c).

Offline profiling grows costly at scale.

Finding the best static split offline also becomes expensive as the cluster grows. A cluster of NN nodes with gg GPUs each has N−1N-1 candidate splits, and evaluating one candidate replays the whole trace of length TT on all N​gNg GPUs, together with a warmup of length TwT_{\mathrm{w}}. An exhaustive search thus costs (N−1)​(T+Tw)​N​g(N-1)(T+T_{\mathrm{w}})Ng GPU-hours, or O⁡(N2​g​T)O(N^{2}gT). A binary search compares two adjacent splits at each of its ⌈log2⁡(N−1)⌉\lceil\log_{2}(N-1)\rceil steps and costs O⁡(N​g​T​log⁡N)O(NgT\log N). For the three-hour CC trace on 256 GPUs, N=64N=64 and Tw=0.5T_{\mathrm{w}}=0.5 h, so each candidate costs 896 GPU-hours. The binary search takes 12 runs, or 10,752 GPU-hours, which is 14×\times the 768 GPU-hours of serving the trace once. The exhaustive search takes 56,448 GPU-hours. Three factors raise these costs further. First, a binary search assumes that throughput first rises and then falls with the number of prefill nodes, yet the throughput in Figure D.1a rises again from a P/D ratio of 0.78 to 1.00. A binary search can thus stop at a local optimum, and a reliable search falls back to the exhaustive one. Second, adjacent splits differ by only a few percent, for example 3% between P/D ratios of 0.45 and 0.60, which is comparable to the variation between runs. Each candidate then needs repeated runs, which multiplies the cost. Third, the search must recur for every new workload composition. A best split per planning window costs even more, since the searches of different windows visit different splits and together approach all N−1N-1 candidates. Evolving Infra instead evaluates the N−1N-1 candidates with its iteration-time models on mm slices at the end of each window, which takes O⁡(N​m)O(Nm) arithmetic on a CPU and no extra GPU time.

Simulation setup.

We further simulate a cluster of 3,072 GB300 GPUs with Frontier [16], a discrete-event simulator for LLM serving. We profile the prefill and decode iterations of GLM-5.2 offline on our GB300 nodes and supply these profiles to the simulator. Frontier models KV caching only within GPU memory, and we extend it with the shared host-memory KV pool and the asynchronous fetches of Section 4.2. Since Evolving Infra fetches remote KV while a request waits in the queue, the simulator assumes that each fetch completes before the prefill of its request begins and charges the fetch no time. We replay the Claude Code and Codex traces over 24 hours with about 10 concurrent agents per GPU, or 30,720 agents in total.

Hierarchical scheduling.

A single router cannot monitor every node of a cluster with thousands of GPUs. We therefore divide the cluster into 8 partitions of 384 GPUs, each with its own router, planner, and KV directory (Figure D.2). Constraints such as region and hardware bind each user to one partition, and each partition thus serves its own subset of agents.

Local shifts under a stable aggregate.

Across all partitions, the aggregate workload stays nearly constant, and the PD ratio of the cluster varies by only 7% over the trace. A static split, however, leaves 2 of the 8 partitions severely imbalanced, with queueing times up to 13.9×\times the cluster average. These imbalances rarely stem from bursts of load. While a partition is imbalanced, its total work changes by less than 12.3%, whereas its PD ratio shifts by up to 42.4%. The planner of each partition follows these shifts and improves the throughput by 1.42×\times over a static split.

Summary.

At scale, Evolving Infra corrects the imbalance at two levels. Its router and shared KV pool balance the load among the nodes of a cluster, and the planner of each partition follows the local shifts in PD demand, even when the aggregate workload of the cluster is fixed. Neither level requires offline profiling.

D.3 Open-Loop Replay at Fixed Agent Arrival Rates

The stationary runs of Section 6.2 replay a fixed number of agents in a closed loop, so a slower system also receives requests more slowly, and its queues stay bounded. In production, new agents arrive whether or not earlier ones have finished. This subsection lets agents arrive at a fixed rate and measures the highest rate that each system sustains within latency targets.

Experimental Setup.

We serve the Claude Code trace with GLM-5.2 on 36 GB300 GPUs with the models and hardware of Section 6.1. New agents arrive in a Poisson process at 0.5 to 1.5 agents per minute in steps of 0.25, and all systems replay the same arrivals at each rate. Within an agent, requests follow the trace as in the stationary runs: each is sent once the request it depends on completes and the recorded delay elapses. At most 258 agents run at once, and the time that an agent waits for admission counts toward the TTFT and E2E latency of its first request. A system sustains a rate if its P50 and P95 TTFT stay within 5 s and 15 s, its P50 E2E latency stays within 10 s, it admits at least 90% of the arriving agents, and fewer than 0.5% of its requests fail. We compare Evolving Infra, which starts from 4P5D, with two baselines of Section 6.1: SGLang PD disaggregation at 4P5D, the best closed-loop static split for CC (3(b)), and Dynamo, which starts from 6P3D. In the closed-loop runs of Section 6.4, the initial split changes the mean E2E latency of Evolving Infra by at most 1.8%. We score minutes 30 to 90 of each run, and each configuration runs once.

Results.

Evolving Infra sustains 1.0 agents per minute, twice the rate of static 4P5D, whereas Dynamo misses the targets at every rate, with a P95 TTFT of 22.0 s already at 0.5 agents per minute (Table D.2). At 1.0 agents per minute, Evolving Infra keeps the P95 TTFT at 12.3 s, 11.3×\times and 9.9×\times lower than that of static 4P5D and Dynamo, respectively. As the arrival rate grows, its planner gives prefill more nodes: 2–3 at 0.5 agents per minute, 3–4 at 1.0, 5 at 1.25, and 6–7 at 1.5. Evolving Infra misses the targets at 0.75 agents per minute, although it meets them at 1.0, because of a single planner switch: at minute 75, the planner moves to 2P7D, and prefill requests queue for 120–275 s at P95 until it adds prefill nodes back at minute 85. Before this switch, the run meets every target, with a P95 TTFT of 14.0 s instead of 17.8 s.

D.4 Compatibility with Heterogeneous Parallelism

The best parallelism can differ between prefill and decode. For example, Huawei’s xDeepServe serves DeepSeek with tensor parallelism (TP) in prefill and attention data parallelism (ADP) in decode, because the two phases see different sequence lengths and ADP avoids duplicating the MLA KV cache [71]. SGLang and vLLM, however, choose parallelism strategy with launch arguments [56, 65], so a node that switches between them must relaunch its engine. The symmetric engine of Evolving Infra can avoid this relaunch, because where a node places its weights can be decoupled from how it computes with them: a node can hold the union of the weights that both phases need and switch phases by changing only its computation path, without moving any weights. The extra weights take a small share of GPU memory, and the KV cache of Evolving Infra lies mostly in abundant host memory, which holds four times as much KV as GPU memory (Section 6.1).

Experimental Setup.

We serve GLM-5.2 [18] on six 8×\timesB200 nodes, with TP8 on prefill nodes and ADP8 on decode nodes, and run BrowseComp agents [67], which can only spawn sub-agents, for two hours. We compare Evolving Infra with Dynamo [40] and the best static split, and Evolving Infra and Dynamo both start from 4P2D. In this deployment, the two phases differ only in the attention layers, and the MoE layers use the same parallelism in both. Under ADP, every GPU holds all attention weights, so it also holds the slice that TP assigns to it. Each node of Evolving Infra therefore keeps the ADP layout of the attention weights in both phases: it computes attention with TP in prefill and with ADP in decode, and a switch changes only which of the two it runs. With FP8 attention weights, this layout takes about 10 GB more per GPU than TP alone, or 6% of the memory of a B200 GPU. The planner needs no change, because it fits the iteration-time coefficients of each node online, and these coefficients already depend on the parallelism of the node (Section 5.1).

Results.

As Table D.3 shows, Evolving Infra moves to 2P4D, the best static split, and reaches a mean E2E latency of 15.9 s, within 1.3% of the 15.7 s of that split, which requires profiling each split offline. Switching engines takes Evolving Infra 27 s in total over the two hours. Dynamo ends at 3P3D with a mean E2E latency of 21.9 s, 38% higher than that of Evolving Infra. It spends 913 s, 34×\times as long, switching engines, because it relaunches the worker of a node at every phase switch (Section 3.1).

Wide expert parallelism.

The same decoupling carries over to wide EP, where one engine spans an EP group of several nodes and attention runs with ADP. Under wide EP, the two phases use groups of different sizes and different communication kernels. SGLang, for example, evaluates prefill on 4-node groups with kernels built for throughput, and decode on 9-node groups with low-latency kernels captured in CUDA graphs [61]. A phase switch therefore moves a node from a group of one phase to a group of the other. Elastic EP performs such a move without a restart [2], but it transfers weights: when vLLM grows a DeepSeek-V4-Pro group from 16 to 20 GB200 GPUs, the scale-up takes 92 s in total to transfer weights, warm up, and capture CUDA graphs [3]. Evolving Infra avoids most of this weight transfer by again holding the union of what both groups need. Every node already holds the non-expert weights. For the experts, each group keeps two copies of every expert on different nodes, so each GPU holds twice its share. A node can then leave a group without taking away the last copy of any expert, and it can join any group at least half as large as its old one by serving experts that it already holds. For GLM-5.2 with NVFP4 experts, the second copy takes 7% of B200 memory in a 4-node group and 3% in a 9-node group. Nor does a move reload kernels, because one engine can load the kernels of both phases, as the auto mode of SGLang does [61].

D.5 Comparison with Agent-aware Routers

ThunderAgent [23] pauses agents to prevent KV-cache thrashing (Appendix A.4). Section 3.3 instead attributes the KV reuse that existing systems lose to where they place requests and which KV they evict. This subsection tests which explanation holds on GB300 nodes by comparing ThunderAgent with cache-aware routing and Evolving Infra.

Experimental Setup.

We serve the Claude Code trace with 126 concurrent agents on 36 GB300 GPUs with GLM-5.2, which uses DSA (Appendix B.2). All three configurations keep the split at 4P5D (Table D.4). The first two run the SGLang engines of our baselines (Section 6.1), which evict host memory in LRU order, and differ only in how they choose the prefill node. Each of their prefill nodes caches up to 2.06 million tokens of KV in GPU memory and 8.25 million tokens in host memory, which holds one copy per node (Appendix A.5). For cache-aware routing, we reimplement the policy of the SGLang Model Gateway [58]. For ThunderAgent, we port the program scheduler that Dynamo ships as a router plugin [23, 40] and keep its default thresholds. Since the plugin targets aggregated serving, we apply it to the choice of the prefill node and count host memory in the capacity of a node. ThunderAgent pauses agents that wait for tools once the contexts of the active agents on a node exceed 95% of this capacity. The harness marks the last request of each agent, so ThunderAgent releases finished agents at once. The Evolving Infra configuration is the run with a fixed split in Section 6.4. We score minutes 30 to 85 of each run, and each configuration runs once.

Results.

ThunderAgent pauses no request (Table D.4): by its own estimate, the active agents on a prefill node need at most 86% of its KV capacity (76% on average), below its 95% threshold, since the deduplicated host tier absorbs thrashing (Appendix A.5). It thus performs like cache-aware routing, with 2.6% versus 2.4% lost KV reuse, 0.95×\times the throughput, and 1.14×\times the mean TTFT. With the same split and host-memory ratio, Evolving Infra achieves 1.35×\times the throughput and 0.29×\times the mean TTFT of cache-aware routing and loses only 0.7% of the KV reuse, because its prefill nodes fetch KV from any node that holds it (Section 4.2) and evict first the copies that no active branch references (Section 4.3). Its higher TPOT coincides with larger decode batches, and this comparison does not separate the effects of routing and the data plane. On GB300 nodes, KV reuse therefore depends on where KV resides and which copies host memory keeps, not on KV capacity (Section 3.3).

D.6 Async KV Fetching

When a prefill node fetches KV from host memory, it restores the KV into GPU memory and broadcasts it to all GPUs of the node (Section 4.2). This subsection compares the load-back of upstream SGLang with the asynchronous KV fetching of Evolving Infra.

Experimental Setup.

We use the setup of Appendix D.5: the Claude Code trace with 126 concurrent agents, GLM-5.2 on 36 GB300 GPUs, a fixed 4P5D split, and deduplicated host memory (Appendix A.5). The router uses cache-aware routing for prefill nodes and round-robin for decode nodes in both runs, and only the engine data plane differs. Upstream SGLang broadcasts the KV to the GPUs of the node with NCCL collectives, which share the GPUs with the prefill computation. Evolving Infra moves the KV between GPUs with their copy engines over NVLink while the request waits in the queue, and its decode nodes write KV through to host memory with a GPU kernel that does not block the scheduler. We score minutes 30 to 85 of each run, and each configuration runs once.

Results.

With the same routing, the asynchronous load-back of Evolving Infra cuts the idle GPU time of prefill nodes from 23.6% to 14.4% and achieves 1.12×\times the throughput of upstream SGLang (Table D.5). Mean and P95 TTFT drop by 23% and 24%, and E2E latency by 18% and 21%, although Evolving Infra serves 15% more uncached prompt tokens per second. TPOT stays within 3%. In upstream SGLang, the fetch delays prefill substantially. A prefill node must load the fetched KV into GPU memory before the layers that read it can run, and the NCCL broadcast of this KV shares the GPUs with the prefill computation. As a result, 93% of its prefill iterations wait more than 10 ms before they start, and waiting for the load-back alone takes up to 8% of the prefill GPU time, about 0.3 s for each iteration that consumes fetched KV. These waits add to the queueing delay of every request that fetches its prefix (Section 3.3).

Fetches on decode nodes.

The same runs show why the decode nodes of Evolving Infra only write to the pool (Section 4.2). In upstream SGLang, a decode node also loads reusable KV from its host memory, and the whole batch of the node waits for the load. Decode iterations that start while a load-back is in flight leave the GPUs idle 58.7% of the time, with a mean gap of 82 ms before the forward, about 19 times the mean TPOT of 4.4 ms, against 6.9% for the other decode iterations. Such iterations are rare (0.5% of decode iterations), but each one stalls every request on the node.

Fetches between prefill nodes.

A prefill node may receive a request whose prefix KV resides in the host memory of another prefill node. The node then fetches this KV into its own host memory over RDMA (Section 4.2). We profile these fetches in the run without online phase-split adaptation (8(b)) from minute 30 to minute 85. As Figure D.3 shows, the fetch time grows almost linearly with the number of fetched tokens. Each token carries 54.6 KB of KV, and the RDMA transfer reaches about 52 GB/s for large fetches. A fetch of 64K–128K tokens therefore takes 129 ms at the median. Most fetches are much smaller. For the 92% of fetches with fewer than 16K tokens, the median fetch time is 7 ms. Evolving Infra starts the fetch as soon as the request arrives at the prefill node that serves it. The fetch therefore overlaps with the queueing delay of the request, i.e., the time from this arrival to the start of its prefill. The median queueing delay is 0.7–2.2 s, at least 3.9 times the median fetch time for every fetch size. A fetch that starts only when the prefill begins would instead add its full time to the TTFT.

Appendix E Additional Details

This section gives the three algorithms of Evolving Infra in pseudocode. Algorithm E.1 and Algorithm E.2 implement the branch counts of the cluster-wide KV directory (Section 4.3) and the host-memory eviction of Section 5.3. Algorithm E.3 combines the routing of Section 5.3 (inner loop) with the phase-split planner of Section 5.2 (outer loop).

E.1 Branch and version identifiers

A branch is an independently maintained context and its sequence of requests (Section 1). The harness tags each request with the ID β\beta of the branch that issues it. When it forks a context or spawns a sub-agent, it uses a new ID for the new branch, and it reports when a branch finishes. The router keeps, for each branch, its version vβv_{\beta}, the prefix-tree path πβ\pi_{\beta} of its last request, and the nodes NβN_{\beta} where it holds counts. A path is the sequence of KV blocks of a context in the prefix tree of the KV directory. The version tells an appended context from a rewritten one (Algorithm E.1): a request that only appends tokens extends the previous path and keeps the version, whereas a request whose context was rewritten, e.g. by compaction, leaves the previous path and increments the version.

A forked branch starts with a new ID and an empty previous path, so the node that serves it adds one count to every block that it reuses from its parent. A sub-agent starts a new context, so its blocks are new to the tree. Neither case changes the counts of the parent branch.

E.2 Branch counts and host-memory eviction

The directory keeps, for each block bb and each node nn that holds it, the count Rb,nR_{b,n} of active branches that reference bb on nn. Algorithm E.2 updates these counts from the output of Algorithm E.1 and from KV transfers, and each node evicts its host blocks in the order that the counts give (Section 5.3).

In Algorithm E.2, TbT_{b} is the last access time of block bb and the minimum follows lexicographic order. A block that an active branch still references on nn is evicted only after no zero-count block remains, which keeps the KV of a branch that waits for a tool and evicts the history that compaction replaced or the source copy of a moved branch.

E.3 Routing and phase-split planning

Algorithm E.3runs two loops. The inner loop routes each request to the prefill node with the shortest predicted TTFT, Equation (7). For each prefill node nn, the router forms the work of the request on nn: the cached prefix tc,nt_{\mathrm{c},n} is the longest prefix that the KV directory finds on nn or on another node, of which xnx_{n} tokens must be fetched from another node, and tuc,nt_{\mathrm{uc},n} counts the remaining input tokens. The router reads the running batch and the queue of nn from the latest state that nn reports, and adds the requests that it has sent to nn but that nn has not reported yet. It sums the service times of Equation (3) to predict the wait W^n\hat{W}_{n} before the request starts. The fetch runs while the request waits, so only the part of the fetch time τ⁡(xn)\tau(x_{n}) that exceeds the wait adds to the prediction. The prediction ends when the prefill of the request finishes, so it leaves out the first decode iteration, which is the same on every prefill node. Our implementation evaluates the sum by replaying the chunked prefill iterations of nn in arrival order, which also accounts for requests that share an iteration. The decode node is bound when the prefill starts. The outer loop is the planner of Section 5.2.

Parameters of our runs. Each prefill node reports its state at every iteration launch, and the router uses a state only if it is at most 5 s old. The chunk size is 8,192 tokens. τ⁡(x)=0.45​s+1​μ​s⋅x\tau(x)=0.45\,\mathrm{s}+1\,\mu\mathrm{s}\cdot x for x≥512x\geq 512 tokens (no fetch below 512 tokens). The router also adds to T^n\hat{T}_{n} a copy price proportional to xnx_{n}, which charges the duplicate KV that a fetch creates. Tlearn=1,800T_{\mathrm{learn}}=1{,}800 s, Twin=600T_{\mathrm{win}}=600 s, and 60-s slices, so m=10m=10 for a full window. The planner skips the 120 s after each switch.
